title: Jury makes recommendations following inquest into 2018 shooting death in Nanaimo
subtitle: A coroner's inquest into the shooting death of a man at the Departure Bay ferry terminal in Nanaimo in 2018 has wrapped up, with the jury providing two recommendations.
article: This story contains the subject of suicide.
A coroner's inquest into the shooting death of a man at the Departure Bay ferry terminal in Nanaimo in 2018 has wrapped up, with the jury providing two recommendations.
On May 8, 2018, 39-year-old Jerry Smallwood was driving off the ferry in Nanaimo when he was boxed in by undercover RCMP vehicles who were investigating him for a violent carjacking in Penticton.
Once his car was boxed in, he raised a gun and shot himself in the head, while two officers also shot him multiple times.
"Within minutes, everything took place. The bang, the gunshots," one witness told CHEK News at the time.
Now, some six years later, the coroner's inquest into his death has finished, with the jury presenting two recommendations Tuesday.
The first recommendation is that advanced care paramedics be called whenever there are "planned apprehensions where the subject may be armed," instead of primary care paramedics.
Advanced care paramedics have an additional 18 to 24 months of training compared to primary care paramedics, including managing critically injured patients.

The jury says it's making this recommendation since in this case only primary care paramedics were initially called, and there was some delay in transporting Smallwood to hospital since advanced care paramedics were requested later.

The second recommendation is for police to "expedite regional based full-time ERT teams (Emergency Response Teams), including on Vancouver Island, and continue to supplement the teams with ERT-trained part-time members."

The reason for this recommendation is because ERT members responding to the incident had to be supplemented by plain clothes officers since there were not enough ERT members available, according to the jury.
When the inquest began last week, Smallwood's mother, Sharon Smallwood, said that he was a "happy little boy" who had a normal upbringing in Winnipeg.
Things changed, however, when he suffered a back injury at work, which led to the use of prescription drugs and eventually street drugs.
She said her son became depressed "dealing with the pain and dealing with Worker's Compensation."
A coroner's inquest is called whenever a dearth occurs while a person is detained by or in the custody of a peace officer.

The inquests serve three main purposes - to determine the facts and classification of the death - to make recommendations based on evidence where appropriate, and to ensure public confidence in the circumstances surrounding the death.
On Tuesday, the jury classified Smallwood's death as suicide.
It was the same conclusion that that the Independent Investigations Office of B.C. came to in its report on the incident in 2018.
